definition: The principle that, among models achieving similar performance, the simpler one should generally be preferred, as it is more likely to generalize well.
details: Occam's Razor informs regularization techniques and model-selection practices in machine learning, reflecting the intuition that simpler explanations are less likely to merely be fitting noise in the training data.

explainer.lead: Occam's Razor in machine learning holds that among models with similar performance, the simpler one should generally be preferred. It matters because simpler models are more likely to generalize well.

tiers.eli5: If two answers explain the same thing equally well, trust the simpler one, because the complicated one may just be memorising noise.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers apply it through regularization and model selection; a common pitfall is over-simplifying when the task genuinely needs a more complex model.
tiers.paperLevel: A preference rule: for models of comparable performance, choose the simpler; it motivates regularization and model-selection practices and rests on the intuition that simpler explanations are less likely to fit noise.

explainer.example: Two classifiers score alike on validation data, and the one with fewer parameters is chosen.
